content: Bioinorganic chemistry is a specialized discipline that focuses on the study of metal-containing molecules within biological systems. This field examines the role of metal ions in biochemical processes, including their regulation and utilization. Many naturally occurring biological processes, such as respiration, rely on molecules containing inorganic elements, such as metalloproteins. Bioinorganic chemistry investigates these natural processes in detail. The field has evolved from ongoing research in inorganic chemistry and its significant connections to biological chemistry. As an interdisciplinary area combining biochemistry and inorganic chemistry, bioinorganic chemistry is crucial for understanding the roles of electron-transfer proteins, substrate binding and activation, atom and group transfer reactions, and the properties of metals in biological systems. History Paul Ehrlich demonstrated the medical relevance of metals, or at least metalloids, by using organoarsenic compounds (arsenicals) to treat syphilis. This work laid the foundation for the field, which gained further prominence with Rosenberg’s discovery of the anti-cancer properties of cisplatin (cis-PtCl₂(NH₃)₂). The first protein ever crystallized was urease, which was later shown to contain nickel at its active site. Vitamin B₁₂, a treatment for pernicious anemia, was revealed through crystallographic studies by Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin to contain cobalt within a corrin macrocycle. The Watson-Crick model of DNA highlighted the structural importance of phosphate-containing polymers in biological systems. Research Areas Bioinorganic chemistry encompasses several distinct areas of interest: 1. Metal Ion Transport and Storage: This includes proteins and small molecules, such as Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, vacuoles, and siderophores, which regulate the concentration of metal ions within cells. 2. Metallohydrolase Enzymes: These enzymes interact with water and substrates, performing hydrolytic reactions. Examples include carbonic anhydrase, metallophosphatases, and metalloproteinases. 3. Metal-Containing Electron Transfer Proteins: These proteins are categorized into three major classes: Iron-sulfur proteins, such as rubredoxins, ferredoxins, Rieske proteins, and aconitases. Blue copper proteins. Cytochromes. These proteins complement non-metal electron transporters like NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). 4. Oxygen Transport and Activation Proteins: These systems extensively utilize metals such as iron, copper, and manganese. Hemoglobin, which uses heme for oxygen transport in red blood cells, is perhaps the most well-known metal system in biology. Other oxygen transport systems include myoglobin, hemocyanin, and hemerythrin. Oxidases and oxygenases, such as cytochrome c oxidase and cytochrome P450 oxidases, exploit oxygen for energy generation or small molecule oxidation. Methane monooxygenase is another example. 5. Protective Metalloproteins: Some metalloproteins protect biological systems from the harmful effects of oxygen and reactive oxygen species, such as hydrogen peroxide. Examples include peroxidases, catalases, and superoxide dismutases. The oxygen-evolving complex in plants, part of the photosynthetic machinery, produces oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis. 6. Bioorganometallic Systems: These include enzymes like hydrogenases and methylcobalamin, which are biological examples of organometallic chemistry. 7. Nitrogen Metabolism Pathways: These pathways heavily rely on metals. Nitrogenase is a well-known metalloprotein involved in nitrogen metabolism. More recently, the cardiovascular and neuronal significance of nitric oxide has been studied, including the role of nitric oxide synthase in its production. 8. Metals in Medicine: This area focuses on the design and mechanisms of action of metal-containing pharmaceuticals and compounds that interact with endogenous metal ions in enzyme active sites. Examples include platinum and ruthenium anti-cancer drugs, chelating agents, gold drug chaperones, and gadolinium-based contrast agents used in medical imaging.
